results.summary: Wormy is a simple snake-like game where a worm grows by eating and must avoid colliding with itself. It is played using four buttons that are debounced and synchronized to prevent metastability. The game state is displayed on a 4x4 grid of LEDs driven by a multiplexing scheme using eight outputs. The design is educational, explaining concepts such as multiplexing and button filtering, and is tested by observing a moving and growing pixel after reset.

This design is a 3-bit dot operation calculator that performs multiplication or division based on an opcode input. It takes two 3-bit operands and outputs the product or quotient and remainder on six output pins. The design is intended for educational use and requires external switches and LEDs for input and output. The documentation is minimal, providing only basic operation and testing instructions.

This is a tiny logic analyzer that samples a single digital input and displays its current state and edge events on a 7-segment display. It uses a shift register to detect rising and falling edges, and counters to extend the display duration for visibility. The design requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board, and can be tested using a dip switch as the data input. It is intended as a simple debugging tool for observing signal transitions.

This project implements a UART interface that allows reading and writing internal registers via a simple two-byte protocol. It includes a signature, an internal register, an LED register, and input status readback. The design is tested by sending specific command bytes and observing responses, with initial LED display showing three horizontal segments. It requires a UART host for communication and provides a basic register access mechanism.

This is a hardware implementation of the HOVALAAG VLIW processor, originally from a programming game. It uses 32-bit instructions and 12-bit I/O, with data transferred over 5 clocks per processor clock. The design can be programmed using an external assembler and tested by loading programs and observing outputs. It is notable for being a faithful recreation of a game CPU in hardware.

This design is a wall clock with an alarm feature, using an 8-digit 7-segment display multiplexed via time-division. It includes three buttons for setting the time and alarm. The documentation is very sparse, providing only a brief description and no detailed testing instructions. It requires external hardware such as a 7-segment display and buttons.

Solo Squash is a single-player Pong-like game that outputs a 640x480 VGA signal and simple tones. The player controls a paddle to keep a ball bouncing within a playfield, with no score. The design includes a leading zero counter experiment that outputs on the bidirectional pins. It requires external VGA connections with resistors, buttons, and an optional speaker.

This project is an attempt to recreate the NES APU pulse oscillator using XLS. It implements a base oscillator with adjustable period and duty cycle, and outputs multiple octave-shifted signals. The design requires external hardware such as an ADC, potentiometers, and a speaker for testing. It is notable for using XLS for hardware generation and targeting audio synthesis.

AS1802 is an implementation of the CDP1802 microprocessor architecture with a Q-SPI memory interface. It supports external ROM and RAM chips for program and data storage, and includes UART and general-purpose I/O. The design is tested by connecting a W25Q-series ROM preloaded with a program that blinks the Q output. It is notable for being a complete CPU with external memory support.

This module implements a 16x7 content-addressable memory (CAM) that is addressed by its contents rather than explicit addresses. It uses behavioral Verilog to infer comparators and registers, and supports writing with automatic replacement of the oldest entry. The design is tested using a cocotb testbench and requires no external hardware. It is notable for being a simple, purely behavioral CAM implementation.
